payload.name: Expand recommendation queries beyond attribute terms
payload.description: When a question asks what item a person suggested or recommended (possibly with descriptive attributes), use this to retrieve memories with recommendation phrasing and avoid over-anchoring on the attributes.
content: If a question asks what a person suggested, recommended, or endorsed as fitting some description (e.g., 'awesome open-world game for the Nintendo Switch'), do not build all searches around the descriptive terms; the supporting memory may state the recommendation without those terms.

Run an additional memory search using the person's name together with suggestion verbs such as 'recommends', 'suggested', 'suggests', 'advises', and if known the general category of the item (e.g., 'game', 'book'), even if the attribute terms are absent.

Before answering, prefer a memory that explicitly records a recommendation or suggestion over one that merely matches the descriptive attributes; if none of the retrieved memories explicitly state a suggestion, keep searching before answering.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what specific item (game, book, movie, etc.) a person suggested or recommended and includes descriptive attributes, retrieval often over-anchors on the attribute words and misses memories that state the recommendation using verbs like 'recommends' without those attributes. This skill instructs the agent to run additional searches with suggestion verbs and to prefer explicit recommendation evidence over attribute-matching but non-recommendation memories, covering any future question about a person's suggested items.

payload.name: Enumerate additional favorites after partial retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks for a plural list of a person's favorite or liked items and the first search returns some concrete items, run a supplementary preference-term search and aggregate all named candidates before answering.
content: If the question asks for a plural list of a person's favorite/liked items and the first search returns some concrete items, do not answer immediately; run an additional search combining the person's name with preference terms (favorite, likes, prefers, enjoys) and the item category, without restricting memory_kind.

Inspect event-kind memories whose predicate is 'preference' and activity memories where the person made, enjoyed, or suggested an item; if they name a distinct category item, treat it as a candidate favorite and include it in the enumeration.

Before finalizing, aggregate all distinct candidate items from the retrieved memories; include a retrieved item if it fits the category and appears in a favorable context for the person, even if the memory lacks the word 'favorite'.

candidates.solves: Solves plural favorite/like enumerations where initial retrieval returns some items but misses other favorites stored as event-kind preference predicates or activity memories. The diagnosed cause was stopping after the strongest memories instead of re-searching preference terms and aggregating all named candidates. Applies to any topic (desserts, books, foods); not to single-item, yes/no, or non-preference facts.

payload.name: Search emotion/appreciation statements for view questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks how a person views, regards, or thinks of something; before answering, also search for concrete emotion/appreciation expressions such as grateful, thankful, loves, or family.
content: When a question asks how someone views or regards something (e.g., 'what does X view Y as?'), do not rely only on queries containing abstract words like view, perception, or opinion; those words may be absent from stored memories.

Run supplementary searches combining the person with concrete emotion/appreciation/relationship terms (e.g., grateful, thankful, loves, 'part of the family') and with the target entity, and inspect event and preference memories for explicit attitudinal statements.

Before answering, require evidence that states the person's view or feeling explicitly; if retrieved evidence only shows related behaviors or plans (e.g., adopting, volunteering, activities), continue searching instead of inferring the view from behavior alone.

candidates.solves: Questions asking how someone views/regards something can be answered by explicit emotion/framing statements (e.g., grateful, part of the family) that are not retrieved by abstract terms like view or opinion; the agent wrongly inferred the view from behavioral evidence. This skill mandates searching for such expressions and requiring explicit attitudinal evidence before answering, applying to any person/entity view question, not to counts or period activities.

payload.name: Health injury synonym and family-member retrieval
payload.description: When a question asks who was injured, hurt, or affected by a health condition—especially within a family—use synonym expansions for the health event and separate searches for each family member before answering.
content: If a question asks about injuries, accidents, or health problems affecting a person or their family, do not answer from a single search using only the literal wording (e.g., 'injured'); memories may describe the event with related terms such as accident, injury, hurt, surgery, hospital, or specific body parts.

Run at least one supplementary search combining the person's name with synonyms of the health condition (e.g., 'accident', 'injury', 'hurt', 'hospital', 'surgery', 'recovery'), and include queries for each named family member or relation (son, daughter, partner, spouse, child) when the question asks 'who' in a group.

Before answering, check that the retrieved evidence covers every person the question asks about; if only the main subject is found, continue searching with family-relation terms until relevant memories for all individuals are retrieved or exhausted.

candidates.solves: This addresses retrieval failures when a health/injury question about a person and their relatives is answered from the first search that matches only the main subject's own injury. Memories about relatives often use different vocabulary (accident, injury, hurt) or are stored under a family-relation term, so the rule requires synonym-expanded and per-relative searches before answering. It applies to any future question asking who in a family or group was injured, hurt, or had a health issue; it is not for general activity, preference, or theme questions that have no injury/health component.

payload.name: SearchEventMemoriesForSocialConnectionsBesides
payload.description: When a question asks whether someone has friends, teammates, or other social connections besides/apart from a named person, search event memories for team/group activities before concluding no.
content: When a question asks whether someone has friends, teammates, or other social connections 'besides', 'apart from', or 'other than' a named person, do not restrict retrieval to relationship memories or build the query only around 'friend' and the excluded person.

Broaden memory_kinds to include event (and profile/preference when relevant) and run searches with group-activity terms such as team, teammate, club, group, member, tournament, competition, class, coworker, together, plus the person's known activity context.

Inspect any returned event/activity memories for participation that implies other people (e.g., winning a team tournament, joining a club); such memories are valid evidence of social connections beyond the named person.
Before answering 'no' or 'only the named person', discard results that are only about the excluded person and, if no group-activity evidence appeared, try additional expansions.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: retrieval was restricted to relationship memories and queries dominated by 'friend' plus the excluded person, so an event memory of the person winning a team tournament was missed even though it implies teammates. The abstract failure is treating social-proof questions as needing explicit relationship records, when group or team events are often the only evidence of additional social ties. This rule applies to any future 'does X have friends/connections besides Y' question across topics.

payload.name: Verify general hobbies before inferred recovery activity
payload.description: When a question asks what activity someone does during a recovery/healing period, search for the person's general hobbies and prefer an explicitly stated hobby over an inferred low-impact plan when both appear in retrieved memories.
content: If a translated question asks what activity a person does while healing/recovering from an injury, run a supplementary search with queries like '<person> hobbies' and '<person> enjoys [hobby]' in addition to any recovery-focused search.

When retrieved memories include both a general hobby (e.g., 'enjoys [activity] as a way to relax') and an inferred low-impact plan (e.g., 'intends to continue with low-impact activities like swimming'), treat the directly stated hobby as stronger evidence for the activity during the recovery period unless the plan explicitly names the activity.

Before answering, confirm the chosen activity is explicitly named in at least one retrieved memory; if only a tentative or inferred activity is present, expand search with the concrete hobby term before finalizing.

candidates.solves: When answering what activity a person does while healing or recovering from an injury, do not trust the first retrieved plan/event memory that mentions any low-impact or recovery-related activity; the person's general hobbies (stored independently, possibly as event/preference memories) can be the correct activity. Run supplementary searches using the person's name plus hobby/pastime terms, and if a general hobby memory exists, prefer the directly stated hobby over an inferred plan before answering.

payload.name: Retrieve explicit ailment names for cause-linked health questions
payload.description: When a question asks what ailment or medical condition a person has due to a cause such as weight, stress, or diet, use this skill to broaden retrieval.
content: When a question asks which ailment or medical condition a person faces due to a stated cause, run at least one supplementary search for the person's health-related memories using terms like '<person> health', '<person> doctor', '<person> diagnosis', 'medical condition', or 'ER visit' without repeating the cause qualifier.
Treat event memories that name a specific condition as stronger evidence than generic state memories about health struggles; answer with the named condition when present.

If initial searches return only generic health descriptions, issue further searches for plausible condition terms (e.g., from any symptom or discomfort mentioned) before concluding insufficient evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a specific ailment or medical condition caused by a stated factor (e.g., weight, stress), retrieval often fails because the condition is stored as an event without the causal qualifier. The agent answers with generic health terms instead of the exact condition. This skill instructs broadening to health-related memories and specific condition terms, applicable to any person's health-related questions.

payload.name: Broaden memory kinds for stress-relief queries
payload.description: When a question asks what a person uses to relieve stress, relax, or de-stress, search across all memory kinds including state and plan, not only preference/event.
content: If a question asks about a person's stress relievers, relaxation methods, or ways to unwind, do not restrict memory_kinds to 'preference' and 'event'; include 'state' and 'plan' memories because stress-relief evidence can be stored as emotional states or planned calming activities.

Run supplementary searches with stress/relaxation vocabulary (de-stress, relax, calm, unwind, cope, guilty) across all memory_kinds, and accept indirect evidence such as a person feeling guilty about a comfort behavior or planning an outing to de-stress.

Before answering, verify that state and plan memories were searched; if the initial retrieval lacks them, issue a broader memory_kind search and treat relevant state/plan memories as supporting evidence.

candidates.solves: When a question asks what relieves someone's stress, the agent only searched event/preference memories, missing state memories that imply comfort behaviors and plan memories that express de-stressing outings. The reusable rule is to broaden retrieval across all memory kinds (state, plan, event, preference) and accept indirect evidence of stress relief, such as guilt about an indulgence or a planned calming activity. Applies to any future question about stress relievers, relaxation, unwinding, or coping; not for current-activity or explicit-advice queries already governed by other Skills.

payload.name: Expand health-incident queries with diagnostic terms
payload.description: When a question asks what health scares, medical incidents, or health problems a person or group experienced, retrieve memories that name specific conditions or symptoms, not just memories using the phrase 'health scare'.
content: When the question asks about health scares, health incidents, medical problems, or illnesses experienced by one or more named people, do not rely only on generic 'health scare' or 'health issue' vocabulary. Run additional keyword or structured searches using concrete medical condition and symptom terms (diagnoses, body-part pains, ER or hospital events) and predicate values such as 'health_issue'.
For multi-person questions, run separate searches for each named person in addition to the combined query, because a single combined query can fail to surface each person's specific incident.
Before answering, verify that every named person in the question has retrieved evidence; if a person is missing, issue additional varied searches before finalizing the answer.

candidates.solves: Questions asking what health scares or medical incidents someone experienced can fail when supporting memories record specific diagnoses or symptoms instead of the generic phrase 'health scare'. The diagnosed agent stopped after one broad search and answered from vague health-state memories, missing concrete incident memories for both people. Future questions of this type will benefit from expanding retrieval to diagnostic/symptom vocabulary and from searching for each named person separately before answering.

payload.name: Prefer specific competing interest over generic obligations
payload.description: Use when asked why someone delays, skips, or puts off a regular activity and retrieval surfaces a specific preferred hobby or interest alongside generic obligations; prefer the specific preference as the cause.
content: When explaining why someone delays or skips a recurring activity, if retrieval returns a memory naming a specific preferred activity the person enjoys, answer with that activity as the cause rather than with generic obligations such as work, school, stress, or busyness.

Do not infer that work or other responsibilities caused the delay unless a memory explicitly states that; a preference memory about the alternative activity is sufficient evidence even if it never mentions the delayed activity.

During the competing-interest search, include long-standing commitment terms (e.g., 'passion', 'since age', 'for years') because enrichment memories capturing deep interest are the strongest support for a 'more interested in X' explanation.

candidates.solves: Future 'why does X sometimes put off Y' questions where the true cause is a stronger interest in another activity; runtime searches surface a preference/hobby memory for that activity but the agent answers from generic obligations (work, stress, projects). The rule trains preference of the retrieved specific competing interest over inferred obligations, plus searching for long-standing passion evidence. Boundary: not applicable when a memory explicitly attributes the delay to stated obligations, or when no competing preference memory is retrieved.

payload.name: Expand stress-relief queries with calming vocabulary
payload.description: When a question asks what relieves a person's stress or what they do to relax/unwind/de-stress, expand retrieval with calming/peaceful synonyms and include preference/event memories.
content: If a question asks what relieves someone's stress or what they do to relax, unwind, or de-stress, do not search only the literal words 'stress', 'relieve', or 'relax'. Run at least one supplementary search using calming/peaceful vocabulary (e.g., 'calm', 'peace', 'peaceful', 'finds peace', 'comfort', 'de-stress', 'unwind') combined with the person's name and/or hobby terms, with memory_kinds including 'preference' and 'event'.

When judging evidence sufficiency for these questions, accept activity memories that describe a pastime as calming, peaceful, comforting, or relaxing even if they never mention stress; do not answer only from the most literal search hits.

candidates.solves: For questions asking what relieves a person's stress or what they do to relax/unwind/de-stress, the agent may rely only on literal 'stress reliever' wording and stop after one search, missing preference/event memories that describe activities as calming, peaceful, or comforting. The reusable rule is to broaden retrieval with calming/peaceful vocabulary and accept such implicit evidence, which applies to any future stress-relief or relaxation question.

payload.name: Search emotional outcome memories for activity-effect questions
payload.description: When a question asks what a named activity does to a person or how it makes them feel (e.g., 'What does X's Y make X?'), search for memories explicitly linking that activity to the person's emotional state before answering.
content: If a user asks what a person's activity makes them or how an activity affects their feelings (e.g., 'What does X's Y make X?'), do not stop after retrieving general activity, career, or performance memories that lack an emotional outcome; the answer may be in enrichment memories that state the person's feelings toward the activity.

Before answering, run a supplementary memory search combining the person's name, the activity, and emotion terms (e.g., 'happy', 'joy', 'fulfillment', 'enjoy'), and a search for emotional-state memories (e.g., '<person> feels', '<person> happiness').

Judge evidence sufficiency against the asked effect: if no retrieved memory states that the activity makes the person feel that emotion, do not substitute unrelated traits such as determination or success; keep searching for a direct activity-emotion link.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: a verbatim hybrid search for 'what does X's activity make X' returned activity/career memories but missed enrichment memories that explicitly link the activity to an emotion, so the agent answered from unrelated traits. The reusable failure is answering an activity-effect/emotion question without first checking for a direct activity-emotion link. The proposed rule applies to any future question asking how a person's hobby, work, or activity makes them feel, and supplements the default retrieval with emotion-focused searches and a stricter sufficiency check.

payload.name: Verify per-person evidence for multi-subject attribution questions
payload.description: Use when a question asks why multiple named people admire, find inspiring, like, or otherwise feel about the same person or thing, and retrieved evidence may cover only one of them.
content: Before answering a question that names two or more people as subjects (e.g., 'Why do X and Y admire Z?'), check that the retrieved evidence explicitly covers every named person; if only one is covered, do not answer for the group.

Run an additional hybrid or keyword search for each missing person individually, using '<person> <topic> admires/inspired/likes/enjoys', because the relevant detail may be embedded in a broader preference or event memory.

Answer only with reasons that are explicitly supported for each named person; if a person's reason remains unsupported after expanded searches, state that unsupported portion explicitly instead of borrowing evidence from another person.

candidates.solves: When a question asks why multiple named people feel a certain way about the same person or thing, a single retrieval often returns evidence for only one of them, causing a partial answer. This rule requires verifying and, if needed, expanding retrieval per named person before answering, so future multi-subject attribution questions are answered completely and only from supporting evidence.

payload.name: Search routine activities for grief coping sources
payload.description: When a question asks what helped a person find peace, comfort, or cope during grief or a difficult time, search current routines, activities, and preferences, not only memories that mention the loss.
content: If a question asks what helped someone find peace, comfort, or cope after a loss or difficult time, do not limit retrieval to memories mentioning the grief; run additional hybrid/keyword searches for the person's current routines, activities, hobbies, and places (e.g., yoga, walking, nature, gardening).

Treat recent event and preference memories as evidence even when they do not mention the loss, as long as they explicitly describe peace, calm, clarity, or comfort; prefer the most recent version of each memory.
If the first search returns only memories of the loss itself, broaden the query with activity and interest nouns from the person's profile instead of repeating the same grief-focused query.

candidates.solves: Addresses access failures where a question asks what helped a person find peace or cope during grief, and the agent over-anchors on memories mentioning the loss, missing current routine/activity/preference memories that contain the coping sources. Abstracted from a diagnosis where a nature/outdoor activity memory with peace descriptors was missed because queries focused on grieving. Applies to future 'what helped/comforted during difficult times' questions for any person; not for place-only emotion questions already covered by place-search guidance.

payload.name: Enumerate career-best achievements with superlative synonym searches
payload.description: When a question asks which career-high, personal-best, record, or highest-ever performances someone had, search each metric category and expand with superlative synonyms before answering.
content: When a question asks which career-high, personal-best, record, or 'highest ever' performances/achievements someone had, treat it as an enumeration: the answer may span multiple distinct metric categories (e.g., points, assists, sales, grades), each stored in a separate memory.

After the first retrieval, do not stop at the first memory that literally contains 'career-high' or 'record'. Run additional searches using superlative synonyms (highest, best, most, top, personal best, all-time) combined with likely metric/domain nouns relevant to the person's activity.

Before finalizing, check whether retrieved evidence covers every plausible metric category in the question; if additional metrics or domains remain unsearched, continue searching until no new superlative achievement appears.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: 'which career-high performances' was treated as single-slot; only the memory with literal 'career-high' was used and a different category phrased 'highest ever score' was missed. Because record achievements use varied metric wording, enumerate each category with superlative synonyms and check sufficiency before answering. Applies to list-of-records questions; not single-stat recall.
